title: Melting points within an alkali-metal group
stem:
The table gives rounded melting points of pure elements at ordinary pressure. The metallic model represents each of these Group 1 metals by singly charged positive ions and delocalized electrons. The ion radius increases from lithium to potassium. Reference values are rounded from the Royal Society of Chemistry periodic table.

| Metal | Lithium | Sodium | Potassium |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Melting point / K | 453.7 | 370.9 | 336.5 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage decrease in melting point from lithium to potassium using the kelvin scale.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Account for the trend using the metallic model.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student says that a molten sample of potassium cannot conduct because its lattice has collapsed. Evaluate this prediction.

steps.text: The model contains positive ion cores attracted to delocalized electrons.
At the same ion charge and with one outer electron per atom, increasing ion size increases the characteristic separation and weakens attraction.
Less thermal energy is needed to disrupt the ordered lattice, consistent with the lower melting point.
Melting disrupts the fixed, ordered positions of the ion cores.
Mobile delocalized electrons remain in the liquid.
A molten metal can therefore conduct, even though its conductivity may differ from that of the solid.

title: Which observations identify a metallic solid?
stem:
Three pure, sealed samples of matched dimensions were tested at 25 °C and after melting. Each current was measured with the same applied potential and electrode separation. These simulated tests were conducted under inert conditions. An entry below 0.01 mA means the reading is below the detection limit. Only sample P could be rolled into a thin sheet without fracturing.

| Sample | Current, solid / mA | Current, liquid / mA | Melting point / °C |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| P | 36.0 | 20.0 | 232 |
| Q | <0.01 | 7.20 | 801 |
| R | <0.01 | <0.01 | 81 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the measurements to calculate the ratio of the solid current to the liquid current for P. Deduce whether P is still a conductor after melting.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the metallic model to explain both the conductivity of P as a solid and its response to rolling.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student identifies Q as a metal because its melting point exceeds that of P. Using two observations, assess this conclusion and suggest a more plausible structure for Q.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why the readings alone do not establish that R has absolutely zero conductivity.

steps.text: Divide 36.0 by 20.0.
The ratio is 1.80. The liquid current is well above the detection limit.
Mobile delocalized electrons carry charge through the solid.
Layers of positive ion cores can move relative to one another.
Attraction to the delocalized electrons persists as the layers slide, allowing deformation without shattering.
A high melting point alone can also reflect strong ionic attraction.
Q conducts appreciably only after melting, consistent with ions that are fixed in the solid and mobile in the liquid.
A giant ionic lattice is therefore more plausible than a metallic lattice.
A current below 0.01 mA could be non-zero.
A more sensitive measurement would give a lower upper bound, subject to leakage and noise.

title: Resolving two close melting temperatures
stem:
A school uses one calibrated sensor and the same heating procedure for pure samples of magnesium and aluminium. Each row contains three independent estimates of the onset of melting, in °C. The sensor can have a common offset of up to ±3 °C that is unchanged between metals. These readings are simulated.

| Metal | Run 1 | Run 2 | Run 3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Magnesium | 648 | 651 | 651 |
| Aluminium | 658 | 661 | 661 |

In the simple metallic model, magnesium supplies two outer electrons per atom and aluminium supplies three. The aluminium ion core is smaller.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean melting temperature and the half-range of the three readings for each metal.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the results to judge whether the common sensor offset could explain the observed difference. Distinguish repeatability from accuracy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the direction of the difference using the metallic model. Assess a claim that the third outer electron alone accounts for the measured size of the difference.

steps.text: Magnesium mean 650 °C, aluminium mean 660 °C.
Half the difference between maximum and minimum.
Both half-ranges are 1.5 °C.
The mean difference is 10 °C and the two observed ranges do not overlap.
Adding the same offset to both series cancels in their difference.
Small scatter indicates repeatability, while a common offset may still affect either absolute temperature.
Aluminium has a higher positive core charge and more delocalized electrons per atom in the model.
Its smaller core and greater charge density support stronger electrostatic attraction, consistent with a higher melting point.
Both charge and size vary in this comparison, so the third electron cannot be isolated as the cause.
The simple model gives a qualitative trend and cannot predict a 10 °C difference from these data alone.
